expectations.text: Uses item-specific response scales, or explicitly justifies any agree/disagree items chosen
expectations.evidence: Every substantive item uses item-specific formats ('How would you rate…', 'How comfortable do you feel…', 'How often…') and the rationale section explicitly justifies this choice: 'Every substantive question uses an item-specific response format rather than Likert-type agree/disagree statements.'

expectations.text: Selects a 5- or 7-point scale and gives a reason tied to the construct/population
expectations.evidence: All items use 5-point scales. Rationale states: 'reliability and validity rise as scale points are added, then plateau around 5–7. For attitude/evaluation content, 5 points is defensible and has a practical advantage: every point can be clearly labeled in plain English.'

expectations.text: Fully labels the scale points with words rather than endpoints-only or numbers-only
expectations.evidence: Every scale in the draft is fully labeled with words (e.g., 'Very poor / Poor / Neither good nor poor / Good / Excellent') and the rationale section dedicates a section to explaining why: 'All five response options on every item use words, not numbers.'

expectations.text: Keeps the instrument short and/or explicitly invokes fatigue/length as a reason
expectations.evidence: The rationale states: 'Eight questions (seven closed, one optional open) is deliberately lean. Pulse surveys exist precisely to impose minimal respondent burden on a recurring basis. Adding more items… compounds two risks: (a) fatigue-driven satisficing in the later items… and (b) declining completion rates.'

expectations.text: Handles the sensitive intent-to-leave and speak-up-safety items with placement and/or confidentiality/anonymity framing
expectations.evidence: The survey header states anonymity upfront ('This survey is completely anonymous — no individual responses will ever be shared or attributed'). The rationale explains sensitive items are placed late: 'The survey opens with manager support… and ends with the retention intent item — which is the most personally sensitive question.' A full rationale section on anonymity is also included.

expectations.text: Each drafted item asks about one thing (no double-barreled items spanning the three topics)
expectations.evidence: All seven closed items are single-construct: Q1 (manager support quality), Q2 (feedback frequency), Q3 (workload manageability), Q4 (burnout frequency), Q5 (comfort speaking up), Q6 (likelihood of being heard), Q7 (attrition thought frequency). No item combines two constructs.

expectations.text: Explains at least one format choice in terms of a named bias or the satisficing/cognitive model
expectations.evidence: Multiple named biases are invoked: 'acquiescence bias' (rationale on item-specific scales), 'satisficing' (midpoint section and length section: 'fatigue-driven satisficing'), 'straightlining' risk (format consistency section), 'telescoping' (Q4 reference period section), and 'social deference' (anonymity section).

claims.claim: Saris et al. 2010 and Revilla, Saris & Krosnick 2014 support item-specific formats on data quality grounds
claims.evidence: These are real papers; the citations and their attributed findings are accurate.

claims.claim: Krosnick & Berent (1993) and Menold et al. (2014) show fully verbal labeling raises data quality, especially for lower-education respondents
claims.evidence: These citations are consistent with the published literature on scale labeling.

eval_feedback.overall: No suggestions — all seven assertions are met with substantive evidence. The response is exceptional in depth. Assertion 7 on named biases is particularly discriminating as it requires explicit theoretical grounding, not just correct design choices.
